paragraphs.text: Acts 10: 1–4; Hebrews 6: 10–12; 1 Corinthians 11: 23–There are memorials in heaven and on earth. Much is often made in these circumstances of a person’s memorial. Like Cornelius, our beloved sister, now with Christ, has a memorial in heaven. The irrelevance of a memorial on earth can be appreciated in the light of a memorial in heaven. It was said by the angel to Cornelius, “Thy prayers and thine alms have gone up for a memorial before God”. There are persons whose names are written in heaven, and such have memorials there. They require no memorial service here. Our sister’s life, in which for many years devotion, kindness, prayers, and alms have had a place, has accumulated for her a memorial in heaven. Persons composing the assembly have each a memorial in heaven, where also they themselves will be placed in due course at the coming of the Lord, to be with Him and like Him in glorious conditions eternally.

The passage in Hebrews refers to things which God does not forget, “God is not unrighteous to forget your work, and the love which ye have shewn to his name, having ministered to the saints, and still ministering”. Love to His name finds expression in ministering to the saints.
We may say of many who have gone before us, “having ministered”; but “still ministering”
brings its own challenge and encouragement to us who are alive and remain. Along with this ministration, such as Barzillai rendered in the

wilderness to David and the people (2 Samuel 17: 27–29), we are each to “show the same diligence to the full assurance of hope unto the end”, and thus to lay hold of, and go in for, what is the present purpose of God for us. The believer’s calling is sonship, and the hope of his calling is heaven. It is in this connection that the spirit of longing comes into Paul’s exhortation—his earnest desire for the saints. When the test came, Barzillai did not commit himself but Chimham (whose name means ‘longing’) went over the Jordan to dwell in Jerusalem with David (2 Samuel 19: 38). We are thus now to be committed to our heavenly calling.

Then there is a memorial that will never be in heaven. The Lord Jesus has left His memorial here upon the earth. He has entrusted it to faithful lovers, and it is of this, the most impressive of all memorials, indeed the administrative centre of christianity, that Paul speaks in 1

Corinthians 11. He quotes the Lord’s own words when He instituted the Supper, confirmed to him, and through him to us, from His present position as glorified. His words convey to every one who loves His name, and has His commandments and keeps them, His personal desire that we should call Him to mind. Nor is it irksome to any who truly love Him, that they should fulfil His desire so unmistakably expressed—“The Lord Jesus, in the night in which he was delivered up, took bread, and having given thanks broke it, and said, This is my body, which is for you—this do in remembrance of me”. This memorial will not be needed in heaven, ‘in the peace that His presence shall crown’ (Hymn 139). It is in the local assembly, during the time that He is absent, that we remember Him—“Ye that have escaped the sword, go, stand not still—remember Jehovah from afar, and let Jerusalem come into your mind”, Jeremiah 51: 50.

May the Lord touch every heart, that we may not only be diligent in ministering to the saints, but allow nothing to interfere with our response to His desire to remember Him in the way He has appointed.
Substance of word at the burial of Miss E. M. Ratcliffe, Buckhurst Hill

I have read this sentence because of a preaching by our dear brother, who is now with Christ, and whose body we surround. I was affected in earlier days when he preached from this sentence, “Give place to this man”. I refer to “this man” as alluding to Christ, the Man whom God sets forth so that every one of us might give place to Him. The history of our brother, as sustained through 87 years, witnessed to the way he gave place to Christ and influenced others to do likewise.

There are two features that would cause the heart to give place to Christ, one is who He is, the other is what He has done. We are reminded that, as to who He is, He is “over all, God blessed for ever” (Romans 9: 5)—wondrous fact as to who He is in His Person, unchanged, unchanging, unchangeable: from eternity to eternity He is God, not bounded by dispensations or ages, eternally God. How many scriptures could be brought forward to show the deity of Christ, John 1: 1 reminding us that “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and

the Word was God”. First, His eternal existence; then “the Word was with God”—His distinct personality as in the Deity; and then “the Word was God”—His absolute deity. How strengthening to faith is the precious truth of God as to the glory of the Person of Christ. John 1. Colossians 1, and Hebrews 1 all reminding us of the glory of who He is. Everything must give way to Him, and everything will finally give place to Him.

Death has already given way to Him, because He entered into death as an invader and death did not do battle—death fled—“What aileth thee, thou sea, that thou fleddest? thou Jordan, that thou turnedst back?”, Psalm 114: 5. It is not that Jordan was turned back, but Jordan turned back, that is, Jordan gave way in the presence of the power of the Son of God. It is a wonderful fact that our brother was in the knowledge that Christ had been into death. He enjoyed the forgiveness of sins, enjoyed being justified by faith, enjoyed the knowledge of redeeming love, and the gift of sonship. Our brother has died not as having any fear of it, but as having a link with the Man who has been there before, has faced it, has gone through, and is now glorified. He has broken the power of death, delivering “those who through fear of death through the whole of their life were subject to bondage”, Hebrews 2: 15. What a glorious Man this is, to whom we can give place. Soon creation, soon the nations, will give place to Him when He comes in to manifest His power, to reign from shore to shore. At the present time there are many hearts that are giving place to this Man. He is worthy that He should be honoured, made room for, and given place to, in every heart.
Then there is what He has done that makes Him precious to us. Our brother enjoyed what Christ

had done for him, and he was in the secret of what He will yet do for him, because He will yet come in in power and raise the dead. Think of the power Christ will have in relation to taking the sleeping saints out of the grave. He will come with archangel’s voice and with trump of God and the dead in Christ shall rise first—a glorious matter this as to what Jesus has done, and what He will yet do. And in faith we await Him as Saviour of the body. What our brother still needs is salvation in this sense in which we are now speaking of it. He enjoyed salvation in relation to the perfect work of Christ, but he awaits the full thought of salvation in the change of condition that the Lord Himself will effect when He comes.

So I commend this to all our hearts. That preaching of our beloved brother affected me over thirty years ago, and I have never forgotten it. There are certain things that stay with you. The Spirit of God has His way through the word of God, and through the application of the word in power in the soul, and I commend this to all of us here today, that we give place to this Man. Wonderful glory is His; how heaven has made room for Him up there—
‘Received in glory bright up there,
The Father’s greetings, honours rare,
Are heaped upon His Son’s blest brow;
He is the mighty Victor now’.

Heaven has made room for Him, given place to Him. Soon, as we have said, the nations will give place to Him. Soon creation itself will respond, because when God brings His Firstborn into the habitable world He says, “Let all God’s angels worship him”, Hebrews 1: 6. Think of the angels giving place to Him, of creation itself, the universe, giving place to Him; how fitting and comely it is that we should the more ‘give place to this Man’, in the precious knowledge of who He is and in the appreciation of what He has done. May the Lord bless the word.

articles.title: THE DEATH OF A WORSHIPPER
articles.author: J. A. Gardiner
articles.meeting: Words at the burial of Mr, James Addison

paragraphs.text: The death of any of God’s saints is precious in His sight. Scripture says, “Precious in the sight of Jehovah is the death of his saints”, Psalm.116: 15. Heaven is intensely interested in these occasions, the angels looking on to see the work of God, seeing what God has wrought.

The death of a worshipper is especially precious in the sight of heaven. Our brother was a worshipper, a worshipper of God, a true worshipper, who worshipped in spirit and truth. He worshipped God because he loved Him; he was known of God, because he loved God. The Scripture tells us that “if any one love God, he is known of him”, 1 Corinthians 8: 3. Our brother had his confidence in God. He was a man of experience in the ways of God, like Jacob here, and he shone in the features of fatherhood and godly influence. Like Jacob he could say, ‘Behold I die’. What a triumph that is!—Jacob, an old man, at the end of his days, saying, “Behold, I die”; facing the whole matter in confidence in God, not thinking about himself, but thinking about those he was leaving.
He says, “God will be with you”. What a comfort that is to our beloved sister. In one sense she needs nothing else. The Lord would say that—“God will be with you”. Whatever the days

ahead may be in sorrow and loneliness and weakness, “God will be with you”. How comforting that is! Our confidence is in Christ; we believe in the Lord as to a generation following in the footsteps of their father spiritually and morally. Our brother had no family, but he surely had a family morally and spiritually. I thank God that I have come under his influence in that way. “God will be with you, and bring you again to the land of your fathers”. Jacob is really saying to them, ‘All the promises are secured, secured in Christ’.

There is no vacillation with the Lord Jesus, everything is firm and fixed. He did not become yea and nay, “but yea is in him. For whatever promises of God there are, in him is the yea, and in him the amen, for glory to God by us”, 2 Corinthians 1: 19, 20.

Now Israel says, ‘I have taken something’—I will give you this tract of land which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow. Our brother has left us something, beloved brethren, that he acquired himself. He has handed things down. Our brother has handed down certain features to us, not features, I suppose, that the world would count of much value—he has handed down kindness, compassion, grace, and patience; such precious features as meekness, lowliness of mind, and humility. These are features that in the sight of heaven are of great price; that is what he has given to us; it is what a worshipper has handed on to us; what he has learned of God he has left with us to explore that inheritance.

How beautiful it is to see a man moving in the light of the knowledge of God. Jacob here was superior to Joseph. Joseph was a great man, over the whole land of Egypt, with the whole administrative position at his fingers; and yet he was not as
intelligent as Jacob. Jacob crossed his hands wittingly and it says it was evil in Joseph’s eyes.

How beautifully he adjusts Joseph, “I know, my son, I know” (Genesis 48: 19). He had been that way before; he had been through the whole thing. This section sets out moral and spiritual beauties and glories that belong to the worshipper, features of the kingdom coming to us, the younger subject to the elder, binding on humility one towards another. How beautifully it was found with Jacob. What a history he had, what experience he had, and he says this with the confidence of a heart that is filled with the knowledge of God—“Behold, I die; and God will be with you, and bring you again to the land of your fathers”—bring you into the full gain of His purpose and of all the promises.

So his heart is full in chapter 49; he is blessing his sons; he is blessing them in relation to the whole area of responsibility, telling them what is to come upon them, and that is blessing. If they submitted to it, they would come into the gain of that blessing. Finally it says that “when Jacob had made an end of commanding his sons, he gathered his feet into the bed”. The whole position rightly arranged under God, his pathway over, he gathered his feet into the bed. What feet they had been! What feet our brother’s feet have been! What feet they have been in testimony. The Lord has used him in testimony. Our brother has referred to his service in the glad tidings, and there are those here today who are the fruit of that service, God using him in the preaching, using our sister, too, in the conviction of souls. All that is present today, all that is the influence of a worshipper, the influence of heaven. These are features, beloved brethren, that those of us who are younger may very well emulate and seek to come into the gain of. So it says, “He gathered his feet into the bed,
and expired, and was gathered to his peoples”. What a triumph that is; how wonderful that is—God taking care of a worshipper.

In John 4 we are in this spiritual area, the tract of land that Jacob gave to his son Joseph (John 4: 5). It is not a thing for the future; it is the present appeal of the love of Christ to us—“The hour is coming and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father ...”. Why does the Lord use that word “the true worshippers”? He uses this word ‘true’ in John at least three times—the true worshippers, the true vine, and the true God—because we are in the presence in this gospel of much that is pretentious, much that assumes things; in the presence of Jerusalem. The Lord’s activities in this gospel are largely around Jerusalem, the great area of religious pretension. He does everything Himself in this gospel. He does not accredit anything that is official, but He accredits the true worshippers. “The hour is coming and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth”. It is not a place of worship; it is not that company or this company of brethren; it is the true worshippers, worshipping the Father in spirit and truth. It is not that they belong to this or to that, but they belong to God. And so the Lord says, “God is a spirit; and they who worship him must worship him in spirit and truth”. What an appeal this is to our hearts, beloved brethren.

The Lord has set before us, by way of moral example, what we saw in excellence in the pathway of our beloved brother. That has been left to us that we may seek to grow and develop in it. What is here in testimony is to be added to, and the service of God is to be enriched, enriched in this
beautiful way by the extension of the features which are absolute in Christ in His humanity.
May it be so.

God has peculiar delight in what is living. He is not the God of the dead but of the living. He has operated in Christ and given His Spirit in order that believers might be in life. Morally dead persons yield no fruit for God, but His people are viewed as sons of the resurrection; they are sons of God. The Lord makes a comparison here between the sons of this world and the sons of that world. It is quite clear that there are two worlds in mind. There is this world that is all around us, governed by what is material and natural. The Lord says they, “marry and are given in marriage”, not that there is anything wrong in marriage, but that is their horizon, as far as they go in their outlook. But then the Lord speaks of those “who are counted worthy to have part in that world”. So, beloved brethren, we want to qualify morally to have part in God’s world. The world that is beyond death is marked by life and is related to the living God, to the Lord Jesus, as Son of the living God, while the Holy Spirit is life, the Spirit of life, and the saints are living stones. I would like to be more characteristically a living stone, because God delights in what is living. So the Lord says there are those that morally qualify. They are “counted worthy”, that is on moral grounds.
From one aspect it is all sovereign grace that we have a place with Christ above, pure grace. But there is another side, of which the Lord is speaking here, that of being morally qualified.

Our place in the kingdom is according to our faithfulness here. And the last years of our life are very important. We want to finish like Jacob, a worshipper, leaning on his staff. He would be counted worthy. He had a chequered career, like some of us, but he had a good finish. We who are older want a good finish.

So how wonderful it is to be sons of the resurrection. That means that we belong to the world of resurrection. This world and all that is in it is marked by vanity and moral death; man is so corrupt and such a sinner. So the Lord here speaks of all living to God; “all live for him”. Is it not wonderful that, for example, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are all living to God? They died hundreds of years ago, yet in their spirits they live to God. All the saints that have died live for God. So we want to be in a real way sons of the resurrection, walking in the power of resurrection life, going against the stream, going against what is down here, against what is defiling. So it is quite clear what the Lord says, “He is not God of the dead but of the living”.

I read these verses in Isaiah to show how we are brought into life by discipline, through experience with God. What is christianity if it does not result in christian experience? It is not theory, and it is not just to be a picture on the wall, we are to experience these things. We are to experience communion with the Father and with the Son and with the Holy Spirit. Now Hezekiah received a very solemn word—God told him that he was going to die

and he must set his house in order. I wonder what we would do if we were told we were to die tomorrow. We would think, ‘Well, now, is there anything I have to put right? Is there anything between myself and any brother or sister that I need to put right? Any unrighteousness with any man in the world?’. Because we want all things to be clear; we want to go out with everything clear. Well, this king, when he received this message, prayed and wept, and he was repentant. I know he reminded God of his works, but God did not answer him because of that. God says, “I have seen thy tears”. He looks at our hearts and if we are real in our prayers He will come in and give us an answer. This was a life-and-death matter and, beloved brethren, our christian life is a life-and-death matter; we must not be careless and easy going, we must have exercise and prayer every day. We must draw near to God every day, because the flesh is very strong within us and the devil tries to hinder us from going on. We know how the devil tries to depress us. Perhaps you do not feel well in your health, then the devil may try to depress your mind. Then you may feel you have not the joy you should have. What must we do? Pray! Just turn to the Lord; even though you may cry and weep, turn to the Lord and pray for deliverance. Have we not proved, beloved brethren, that He answers prayer? That is what Hezekiah proved.

The turning point came in his exercises when he stopped talking about himself. There was a lot of ‘I’ with him, you know. And there is a lot of ‘I’ with some of us. He speaks of mourning like the dove—and ‘I’ this and ‘I’ that. Then he gets his eye off himself and speaks of God in love casting his sins behind His back. He got into the love of God. He was getting out of the dull weather into the sunshine of divine love. Divine love is very

liberating, and he got free. Oh let us get free! We need it every day, as having Christ, that glorious Man, before us. And now what does Hezekiah say? “The living, the living, he shall praise thee, as I this day”. You see, it was experience. There is no substitute for experience with God. You look back on your history and you remember when you proved God. You want through deep exercises and the Lord helped you; you came through the dark tunnel and you got free to sing, “The living, the living, he shall praise thee, as I this day”. Let us be more among this living company, for God takes great delight in the responses of His people.

Hezekiah says in Isaiah 38: 20, “Jehovah was purposed to save me”. He is always purposed to save us. He is the God of all encouragement. Mr. Darby remarked that God does not discourage, He always encourages. It is circumstances, the devil, and ourselves that discourage. Then Hezekiah says, “We will play upon my stringed instruments all the days of our life”. He wanted to share his experience with the saints. He is becoming typically now an assembly man, blending in with the brethren in the service of praise. Is it not wonderful to have part in the service of God in praise and worship? It is the fruit of what you have learned in the wilderness with God. “My stringed instruments” would refer to the harp. It involves our affections and feelings. What you learn of God yourself in soul experience should be for the good and encouragement of the brethren.

So may the God of the living encourage every one of us, young and old, even if we are only small, like those gnats in Exodus 8. You will remember that the magicians of Egypt could not bring life in. The gnats are only little creatures, but they are
in life. The magicians could not bring life in. So the way to confound the devil, to confound the enemy, is to be in life. May it be so with us, for His name’s sake.

I had in mind to say a word as to what is profitable. This scripture in John 11 is about the One, Jesus, who was prophetically spoken of as gathering together into one the children of God. Chapter 16 would give us some impression as to how that was to operate by the Holy Spirit being sent here. The thought of profitability is in this. Maybe we have not realised that the presence of the Spirit was to be more profitable even than if the Lord had remained here.

We may have thought that surely there could not be anything to compare with the Lord’s actually being here. How we would have rejoiced if today it had been the Lord Jesus who was to preach the gospel, the Lord Jesus who was to be working miracles here. Could there be anything greater than that? In one sense there could not, and yet the Lord Himself said there was something more profitable. But we will come to that.

Seeing people, bent on pleasure, going by outside reminds me of what is natural in all our hearts—to think of our own profit, what we would ourselves enjoy most. In commerce today what is uppermost in

persons’, minds is profit. It is far more in mind today than it was. There was a great deal done years ago in business that was not solely for profit. Goodwill was one of the important things in business in days gone by. The village shop was not exactly profit-conscious, but today in business, speaking generally, there is one objective and that is profit.
Now God would say that the things that are really going to profit you are not those things at all, because they end in death anyway; they are only for a time. There is a verse which says,

“What shall it profit a man if he gain the whole world and suffer the loss of his soul?”, Mark 8: 36. People say, ‘Well, it is Sunday; I will profit my health and go down to the sea and enjoy God’s creation and profit by it’. God takes account of this, but He would say to you today, ‘I have got something that is far, far more profitable, and I want to interest you in it’.

The first occasion that profit is spoken of in Scripture is where a number of persons were thinking of killing their brother. There was a man whom they got very jealous about; he dreamed dreams and he was a favourite with his father, and they were jealous about this.

They had got their business—we could call it that—shepherding, and why should this man have a coat of many colours? Why should he have a favourite place? So they were jealous, and when he came to them they decided to kill him. They put him in a pit, but then one of them said, ‘Wait a minute, what profit will there be if we do kill him? We shall have got rid of him, but then we are no better off. I have a much better idea. We will sell him for some money. There are some traders coming down who will buy him and we shall get some money; that is much more

profitable’. So, you see, right in the very first book of the Bible we have the natural mind thinking of profit, even trading in human beings. If it is for profit we will do it, and man’s mind has not changed a bit. I do not want to dwell on this side because we are all conscious of this ourselves, but I just want to talk a little about what God has for your profit and mine.

So we come to John 11, and you may remember that in this chapter the Lord had done one of the most wonderful things in His life here. He had actually raised a man from the dead. You think of that! Men just could not take it in when He said that was His intention. Even those who knew Him and loved Him said, ‘But Lord he has been dead four days, his body stinks, how can You do anything about this?’. They did not know what Jesus could do. Well, He raised Lazarus from the grave; then some went to the Pharisees and they had a counsel and they could see that if they let things go on their position would be encroached upon, and where would they be? Here was One who was obviously taking the interest of the crowds, and the chief priests and the Pharisees—the religious element—were losing ground. So they say, “What do we? for this man does many signs? If we let him thus alone, all will believe on him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11: 47, 48). That would be total loss. So what were they to do? One man rises up and says, “Ye know nothing”. ‘Do you not know that it is profitable for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish?’ There is not one other person anywhere who could save you, not one. Not one of us could save ourselves. But one Man could die for the people. Do you know about this one Man who could die for the people? O, friend, it is a thrill to speak about Jesus who

was prepared to die for the people, that you might live, that you might be free, that you might know God’s love. How could you know anything about God’s love if it was not for the Mediator?—“The mediator of God and men one, the man Christ Jesus”, 1 Timothy 2: 5.

So Caiaphas says, “It is profitable for you that one man die for the people, and not that the whole nation perish”. He prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation, “and not for the nation only, but that he should also gather together into one the children of God who were scattered abroad”. Even at that time it says they were scattered abroad; how much more today! But there is one Man who can bring them together, and I believe it is as He who died and rose becomes the centre. Salvation is only through one Man, and it is only through His precious blood that we can know the forgiveness of sins. O, friend, this is the attractive side of this profitability; it is profitable that one Man die for the people. Well, He has died, but how much does His death mean to us? You think of it; the Man who had Himself just raised Lazarus from the dead was about to enter into the very article of death, suffering the death of the cross. Oh what a death it was! What a witness He was as He went down into death. Death had no claim on Him, no one took His life from Him, but He went down into death, as ever obedient to the Father.

Death always has some effect although perhaps less moving to people today than it was for, along with the times in which we live, life has become cheaper; but even so, I think death is still a moving thing to most persons. There is something which halts persons in the presence of death. I shall never forget a tragedy which occurred when I had started work just a few weeks. In a village

where most knew each other a young lady in her late ‘teens was killed in a road accident. For days there was a hush in that village as the reality of that death, which occurred without warning, came home to the inhabitants. That was just one person in a little village. Now in God’s eyes, you know, the death of every person is vitally important. Today a number will die, and some without warning, but heaven will take account of every one. God will feel the death of every person today, because it means the end of life here, and their being ushered into eternity.

But now I want to go back to the death of Jesus, because heaven was never moved more than to take account of the One who belonged to heaven, at whose birth the heavenly host rejoiced, entering into death itself. I often think of how God must have felt as to the way His beloved Son was treated just before His death, the mockery, the unjust trial, and the way He was smitten, spat upon, and belittled. Oh how heaven must have felt it! Then the sufferings of the cross, and His entering into death itself; how heaven felt it! Friend, does it mean much to us, the sufferings and the death of Jesus? There is a book that is well worth reading, ‘The Sufferings of Christ’. The sufferings of Christ were not only at the hands of men, but also at the hands of a holy and righteous God, that the whole question of sin might be settled, never to be raised again for the believer. Personal acceptance of this is one of the things that is going to bring persons together. Jesus died for each one of us here, each one. It does not matter who you are or where you come from, Jesus died for you, and He died for me.
So it is more profitable that He die for the people than that the whole nation die. How true!
We just cannot begin to take in what would have

happened if Jesus had not died. If Jesus had not gone the whole way there would have been no hope for you or me. But He did, bless His name! And now it is left for you and me to believe. He has done the work. You cannot add to that work one iota; it is complete in itself.

But it is left for you and me to believe, and I feel it laid upon me to press the point as to what His work means to you and me. There is no question about it that He died. There is no question about it that He has been raised again, but perhaps there is a question as to whether we believe it; how much we feed upon it; how much it forms something in us. Are we each really sure that He has borne our sins in His body on the cross? Has anyone here any doubt that the holy and righteous God has forgiven them?

In John 16 we have this remarkable verse in which the Lord says it is profitable for them that He goes away, that the Comforter might come, and then the Lord speaks of what the Comforter would do. “When he is come, the Spirit of truth, he shall guide you into all the truth—for he shall not speak from himself; but whatsoever he shall hear he shall speak; and he will announce to you what is coming”. O, friend, do we value the Spirit enough? He has come and made His abode in us. He came in a most outstanding way, as we read in Acts 2, a most remarkable way, and His coming had a most unifying effect, so that even persons who spoke different languages were able to understand what was being said. I do not think that any other incident in the world’s history has done that. It was because of man’s efforts that God brought about the divergence of languages, but it was God’s action in sending the Spirit that for a moment united persons to such an extent that even those who spoke different languages could understand. The incoming of the Spirit in that sense united them, and that is a

remarkable thing. Well, that same blessed Person is here today, and I believe that will have the same uniting effect as we are subject to Him. But, you know, we must revere Him, we must value Him more, so, that He may have a greater place.

The Spirit of God takes a very lowly place. I could not say He does not assert Himself, for He does, but He retains a lowly position, even to the extent of your or my being able to grieve Him. That is a sorrowful possibility, that you and I could grieve Him, so lowly is He. Well, may we value more the presence of the One who has this uniting power, and there is something for us to do in keeping the unity of the Spirit. You may well ask, How do we do that? Well, it is not for me to say now, except to say that we should value the Spirit more, and that in itself will be helping to keep the unity of the Spirit. So there is one Lord, the One who died for us and shed His blood for us, was raised, and is ascended, who is there in heaven on our behalf; one Lord, one faith, one baptism.

The Lord’s coming and His death, and then the coming of the Spirit, have been profitable. As we accept these things, as we understand them, appreciate them, and value them more, may we enter into what, in God’s eyes, is more profitable, so that things here are related to that. It is not wrong at all to be making profits here, but you relate that to what is profitable in God’s eyes, so that what is natural is not the be-all and end-all, but is held in relation to what is profitable in God’s eyes, and what God has given for our profit, God has given us of His Spirit.
May the Lord make these things more real to us. We know these things, but how real are they to us
every day and in every circumstance? May we increasingly know the power and the comfort of the presence of the Spirit, for His name’s sake.

Christ’s love is a present love, so the doxology in Revelation 1: 5, in spite of all the failure yet to be recorded, is “to him who loves us”, the same One who has washed us from our sins in His blood. He has given many tokens of His love. What could be greater than His making known the Father’s name (John 17: 26)? The conversion of Saul (later Paul) indicates Christ’s love for the church, the place the persecuted disciples had in His affections, and His love was further displayed in such a gift being given as the beloved apostle of the gentiles. So the Lord acts still from His place on high, where He has all power, and will order yet that those who are false acknowledge the true object of His affections, the church, which Saul was persecuting (see Revelation 3: 9), of which the Lord could say, “Why dost thou persecute me?”. Saul came to know how the Lord loved her at a time of grace, so that he, too, became more abundantly serviceable, devoted to Christ’s chief interest here. He will serve best who knows Christ’s present love the most.
Kingston, Ont.
Within the gloom of this dark day,
Where nature gropes and finds no way,
That ‘still small voice’ to faith doth say,
‘‘Tis I, be not afraid’.
When billows round our bark appear,
And tempest’s angry voice we hear,
Above it all sounds rich and clear,
‘‘Tis I, be not afraid’.
When troubles gather fierce and strong,
And weary ones for respite long,
This fills the heart with joyful song,
‘‘Tis I, be not afraid’.
When sorrows and afflictions stand
Around the saint on every hand,
By this the spark of faith is fanned,
‘‘Tis I, be not afraid’.
In pain and sickness, or in health,
In greatest poverty, or wealth,
The power of this sweet word is felt,
‘‘Tis I, be not afraid’.
In every circumstance we trace
Thy wisdom, power, and boundless grace.
Who sayest in this desert place,
‘‘Tis I, be not afraid’.
O blessed Lord! we cease to fear,
Our troubles bring Thee still more near,
Where Thy blest voice doth sound more clear,
‘‘Tis I, be not afraid’.

HIDING AND SHOWING It says of John the baptist that “he was in the deserts until the day of his showing to Israel”, Luke 1: 80. It is part of God’s ways, and in His wisdom, that He hides and prepares what He is later to show. It was so with Moses, David, and Paul (see Galatians 1: 17, 18). Uniquely was it so with the Lord Jesus in those hidden thirty years.

If there is to be anything with us that God can ‘show’—can bring forward in testimony and witness before men, or use to demonstrate the truth by way of formation among His people, it can only be as there is a preceding, and accompanying, secret life of communion and experience before God. So let us accept the desert. God allows many things to make us realise that it is a desert through which we are passing. In the acceptance of that there is much blessing, as our roots go down, not into this world, but into our own true soil. How well worth while it is to be “in the deserts” to find that God is there, with the fulness of His resource and blessing. As Mr. Darby’s hymn says—
‘In the desert God will teach thee,
What the God that thou hast found’.
